content:
What is your computer's operating system?

If I understand your situation, you need to keep mail on Yahoo's servers, but you also want to have copies of it on you local computer. Right? If so, setting up an IMAP account in Thunderbird would probably be the best option. IMAP means that the messages and folders on the server are mirrored on your computer. If you delete a message on the server via the Yahoo web mail page, it will be deleted on your computer as well. And vice versa - if you delete it on your computer it will be deleted on the server, too. But you can also copy or move messages to local folders, which exist outside the IMAP account.

Yahoo accepts two different kinds of authentication. The most secure is OAuth2. When you opt for that method, when you first connect with Yahoo you will be asked for your user name and password. Thunderbird will then accept a token from Yahoo that says, 'Yes, I know who you are and I will let you manage your email.' The token is stored locally like a password, but it's not the password.

Yahoo also accepts the older, less secure authentication method, plain old passwords. However, for that, Yahoo requires that you create an "app password" which is distinct from your regular password. Here's an article describing that process:

https://help.yahoo.com/kb/SLN15241.html

I believe that if you use OAuth2 authentication, 2-factor authentication is not relevant.

So, to get this going, download Thunderbird from the official site (https://www.thunderbird.net/en-US/thunderbird/all/). I recommend you install the ESR (Extended Support Release) version rather than the "Release" version - it's more stable. After installing the program, the first time you run the program, you will be prompted to set up your Yahoo account. Thunderbird will choose appropriate settings, including OAuth2, for you based on your @yahoo.com address. You'll be prompted for your Yahoo password (regular, not an 'app password'), and that should be it. You will see all the email and folders in your Yahoo account copied to your computer. You can then manage (read, write, save, delete, etc.) your Yahoo mail on your computer.

content:
I guess the safest way to do that would be to import the messages from all those extraneous profiles into local folders in your primary profile. That will still leave you with the task of sifting through them and deciding which ones to keep or not, but at least they'll all be in one place. Once you're satisfied that you have everything you want, you can then delete the old profiles. This process will use a lot of disc space while you're doing it, but when you're done you will reclaim that space.

To do this, use Thunderbird's Import feature...

- I recommend you first make a backup copy of your current profile before starting, just in case something goes wrong. Actually, you should make regular backups anyway if your email is valuable to you. These articles describe Profiles and how to back them up. Use the instructions for manually backing up large profiles - the built-in export tool has some limitations.

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/profiles-where-thunderbird-stores-user-data

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/thunderbird-export#w_creating-a-backup-of-large-profiles


- Click on <Tools | Import>, then choose "Import from another Thunderbird installation", then "Continue". You will then be presented with a list of your various other profiles. Chose one and click "Continue".

- De-select everything but "Mail Messages" and click "Continue". You'll see a confirmation window and if that looks good, click "Start Import".

You will wind up with all messages from that old profile in a new Local Folder called "Thunderbird Import"

Now repeat the process for every old profile you wish to merge.

After you eventually have deleted anything you don't want to keep, you can delete any unneeded local folders.

Finally, you can delete the old, obsolete profiles. Easiest way to do that is to go to <Help | Troubleshooting Information | Profiles | about:profiles>. You will find a list of all profiles, each with a "Remove" button.

Thunderbird has a hidden preference setting that controls this behavior.

  1. Open Thunderbird Settings. At the top right of the Thunderbird window, click the menu button ≡ > Settings
  2. Scroll to the bottom of the General panel and click Config Editor...
  3. In the search box, paste: mailnews.nav_crosses_folders
  4. Double-click the preference (or click the edit pencil icon) to change its integer value:
  5. Set the value to 0 and press Enter.

Once set to 0, pressing N will continuously jump across folder and account boundaries directly to the next unread message without interruption.
